_note: PLACEHOLDER CONTENT - the reassurance tips and practical guidance here are drafts. The escalation, prescribing, and consent sections in particular need review by a clinician and alignment with local trust policy before real users see them.
tips: Everyone here was exactly this nervous on day one. Nobody expects you to know everything.
Double-checking a prescription is not a weakness. It is the job.
A nurse who has been on this ward ten years knows things you do not. Ask them.
You will make a mistake. What matters is telling someone quickly.
You are allowed to say: I do not know, let me find out.
The jobs list will never be empty. Prioritise the sick patients.
Eat something. You are no use to anyone lightheaded.
sbar: S - Situation: who you are, who the patient is, what is wrong
B - Background: relevant history in two sentences
A - Assessment: your observations and your read on it
R - Recommendation: what you want them to do

specialties.Medicine: Ward rounds start early and move fast. Your job in week one is the jobs list, bloods, and knowing which patients are sick. Write everything down.
specialties.Surgery: Rounds are earlier and shorter. Much of your day is post-op checks, wound reviews, and keeping on top of fluids and pain relief.
specialties.ED: You will see undifferentiated patients with no notes and no diagnosis. Learn the department's triage system early and ask before you discharge anyone.
specialties.Paediatrics: Doses are weight-based and the margin for error is smaller. Always check with someone. Parents are part of the history.

prescribing: Check allergies before every single prescription
Weight-based doses need an actual weight, not an estimate
Check renal function before renally-cleared drugs
If the dose looks unusual, look it up rather than assuming
Sign, date, and write legibly - unclear prescriptions cause errors
night: Find out who your senior is and how to reach them before the shift starts
Get a proper handover, and write it down
Know where the crash trolley is on every ward you cover
Prioritise: sick patients first, then jobs that cannot wait until morning
Take your break. A tired doctor makes worse decisions
ethics: Consent needs capacity, information, and voluntariness - all three
Capacity is decision-specific, not a blanket judgement about a person
Family do not automatically have a right to clinical information
If you are unsure whether someone has capacity, escalate rather than proceed
Document consent conversations, not just the outcome
nobody: Parking permit, and where not to park
Payroll, rota queries, and who to chase
